كَشُوثٌ (S, K) and كُشُوثٌ and كَشُوثَى and كَشُوثَاءُ (of the fem. gender, Ibn-Buzruj, in TA, voce هِنْدَبٌ) and أُكْشُوثٌ but this last is a bad word, (K,) [as also شَكُوثَى and شَكُوثَاءُ,] [A species of cuscuta, or dodder;] a certain plant that clings to the branches of trees, having no root in the earth. (S, K.) [See also الشَّجَرَةُ الخَبِيثَةُ, in art. خبث. And see الفَقْدُ and سَكَرٌ.] ―
-b2- A poet says, “هُوَ الكَشُوثُ فَلَا أَصْلٌ وَلَا وَرَقٌ
وَلَا نَسِيمٌ وَلَا ظِلٌّ وَلَا ثَمَرُ
” [He is the Kashooth: therefore (he has) no root nor leaves nor fragrance, nor shade nor fruit]. (S.)
From An Arabic-English Lexicon (Edward William Lane)
